articles.title: 'Eclipse do século': fenômeno de 2027 terá 6 minutos de escuridão | G1
articles.standfirst: Eclipse solar total de 2 de agosto será o mais longo sobre terra firme desde 1991 e o segundo mais longo do século XXI. Faixa de totalidade cruzará Europa, África e Oriente Médio, mas fenômeno não poderá ser acompanhado do Brasil.
articles.summary: Eclipse solar total de 2 de agosto será o mais longo em terra firme desde 1991 e o segundo mais longo do século XXI. Fenômeno não poderá ser visto do Brasil.
articles.body:
A Lua encobre completamente o Sol durante o eclipse solar total visto de Arija, na Espanha, nesta quarta-feira (12). — Foto: Borja Suarez/Reuters

Salve no seu calendário: apelidado de “ eclipse do século ”, um dos eventos astronômicos mais aguardados dos próximos anos acontecerá em 2 de agosto de 2027 e poderá deixar algumas regiões do planeta no escuro por mais de seis minutos em pleno dia.

No ponto de maior duração, a Lua ficará diante do Sol por 6 minutos e 23 segundos , fazendo deste o segundo eclipse solar total mais longo do século XXI .

O recorde pertence ao eclipse de julho de 2009, que chegou a 6 minutos e 39 segundos .

Há, porém, uma diferença importante entre os dois. Em 2009 , o ponto de duração máxima ficou sobre o Oceano Pacífico. Já em 2027 , áreas em terra terão mais de seis minutos de totalidade.

➡️ Será a maior duração desse tipo sobre terra firme desde 1991 .

🌑 E nenhum eclipse total posterior será mais longo até 2114 , quando um fenômeno previsto para junho daquele ano deverá alcançar 6 minutos e 32 segundos .

A faixa onde o Sol ficará completamente encoberto terá cerca de 258 quilômetros de largura . Ela atravessará o sul da Espanha e seguirá pelo norte da África e pelo Oriente Médio, passando por áreas de Marrocos, Argélia, Tunísia, Líbia, Egito, Arábia Saudita, Iêmen e Somália.

O Egito estará entre os pontos mais privilegiados para acompanhar o fenômeno.

Nas proximidades de Luxor, no sul do país, a totalidade ficará muito perto dos 6 minutos e 23 segundos máximos .

A cidade, às margens do Rio Nilo e próxima ao Vale dos Reis e a alguns dos principais sítios arqueológicos egípcios, já aparece como um dos destinos mais procurados para a data.

Em outros pontos da trajetória, a escuridão também será longa. Benghazi, na Líbia, ficará mais de seis minutos na totalidade.

Em Jeddah, na Arábia Saudita, serão quase seis minutos, e cidades do sul da Espanha e do norte do Marrocos também estarão dentro da faixa.

E a procura por hospedagens nesses lugares já começou. Levantamentos citados pela imprensa internacional mostram hotéis e excursões sendo reservados com meses de antecedência , especialmente no Egito.

O eclipse solar total 'do século' — Foto: Arte/g1

Um eclipse solar total acontece quando a Lua passa entre a Terra e o Sol e, vista de uma determinada região do planeta, encobre completamente o disco solar .

A duração depende de vários fatores. Em agosto de 2027, eles estarão especialmente bem combinados.

Poucas horas antes do eclipse, a Lua estará próxima do perigeu , ponto de sua órbita em que fica mais perto da Terra. Por isso, aparecerá um pouco maior no céu.

A Terra, por outro lado, estará relativamente próxima do afélio , período em que fica mais distante do Sol. Visto daqui, o disco solar parecerá ligeiramente menor.

Além disso, a trajetória da sombra atravessará latitudes baixas, onde o movimento de rotação da Terra ajuda a prolongar o tempo em que uma mesma região permanece dentro da sombra lunar.

Na prática, o eclipse de 2 de agosto de 2027 não poderá ser observado do Brasil .

Sua faixa de totalidade passará muito longe do país.

No entanto, outro eclipse solar meses antes poderá ser observado pelos brasileiros em 6 de fevereiro de 2027 .

Ele será do tipo anular e será visível como parcial em uma área muito maior do território brasileiro.

A Lua encobre completamente o Sol durante o eclipse solar total visto do Observatório Astrofísico de Javalambre, em Arcos de las Salinas, perto de Teruel, na Espanha, nesta quarta-feira (12). — Foto: Christian Hartmann/Reuters

Como observar um eclipse solar com segurança?

Quem estiver na faixa de totalidade precisará usar óculos próprios para eclipses durante toda a fase parcial.

Somente durante a totalidade , quando o Sol estiver completamente encoberto pela Lua, será possível olhar diretamente para o fenômeno sem proteção.

Assim que qualquer parte do Sol reaparecer, os óculos precisam voltar a ser usados.

Óculos escuros comuns , chapas de raio-X e outros filtros improvisados não oferecem proteção adequada.

Durante aqueles poucos minutos de escuridão total, será possível observar a coroa solar, a atmosfera externa do Sol, normalmente escondida pelo intenso brilho da estrela.

articles.title: In 1879, Edwin Hall discovered an electrical effect thought to need a perpendicular magnetic field; 147 years later, scientists have shown it can work with the field in-plane
articles.summary: Science News: For more than a century, the Hall effect has been taught with a simple picture that electricity flows through a material, a magnetic field pushes the .
articles.body: For more than a century, the Hall effect has been taught with a simple picture that electricity flows through a material, a magnetic field pushes the moving charges sideways, and a voltage appears across the material. Now, scientists have found a way to make that familiar phenomenon work in a direction once thought impossible. According to a report published on Science Daily, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have demonstrated an unusual form of the Hall effect in which a magnetic field lying within the plane of a material can produce a measurable Hall response. The discovery, published in Nature Materials, challenges a long-standing assumption in condensed-matter physics and could eventually lead to simpler magnetic sensors capable of detecting fields along multiple directions. According to the online report, Edwin Hall discovered the Hall effect in 1879. In the conventional setup, a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to a material carrying an electric current. The field deflects moving charges, creating a voltage that can be measured across the material. That voltage can reveal valuable information about the material, including the type and concentration of charge carriers and how readily they move. The principle has since become part of everyday technology. Hall-effect sensors are used in applications ranging from automobiles and keyboards to industrial electronics. But Carnegie Mellon researchers working in the Lab for Investigating Quantum Materials, Interfaces and Devices (LIQUID) have now shown that the response does not have to be restricted to the traditional geometry.Turning a theoretical prediction into realityScientists had previously predicted an in-plane anomalous Hall effect, but demonstrating it experimentally proved difficult. The challenge was finding a material system with precisely the right symmetry. The team began with tantalum iridium telluride (TaIrTe₄), a two-dimensional quantum material whose crystal structure can support the unusual response. Researchers reduced it to only a few atomic layers and placed it alongside a magnetic material called chromium germanium telluride (Cr₂Ge₂Te₆), or CGT. Because the two layers sit extremely close together, the magnetic layer transfers its influence to the normally nonmagnetic TaIrTe₄. The result is an atomically thin device with specially engineered electronic and magnetic properties.One device, multiple magnetic directionsInside the resulting structure, researchers detected the familiar Hall signal as well as a second, unconventional signal associated with magnetization lying within the material's plane. That could have significant implications for magnetic sensing. Instead of requiring separate sensors to measure magnetic fields along different axes, a single ultrathin device could potentially detect multiple directions. The researchers say this could enable new forms of vector magnetometry, with applications in electronics, transportation and medical imaging.Why the unusual effect appearsThe experimental work was accompanied by theoretical modeling to understand the physics behind the discovery. Researchers found that combining the two materials reduces the system's symmetry and enables additional spin-orbit coupling at their interface. These interactions become important when CGT becomes ferromagnetic at low temperatures, helping produce the in-plane anomalous Hall response. However, the precise microscopic mechanism is not yet fully settled, and further characterization of few-layer TaIrTe₄ is needed.What comes next?The Carnegie Mellon team is now looking for other combinations of two-dimensional materials that could produce the same effect. Another major goal is determining whether the devices can operate at room temperature.That step will be crucial for any practical technology.For now, the discovery expands the possibilities of a phenomenon first identified nearly 150 years ago — showing that even one of physics' most familiar effects can still have a few surprises hidden in it.Images Credit: Carnegie Mellon and Wikipedia

articles.title: Scientists altered the air around a Wisconsin forest for 11 years; extra CO₂ drove 39% more productivity, but ozone reversed part of the gain
articles.summary: Science News: What happens when young forest communities spend more than a decade growing in air with unusually high levels of carbon dioxide and ozone? Scientists .
articles.body: What happens when young forest communities spend more than a decade growing in air with unusually high levels of carbon dioxide and ozone? Scientists in Wisconsin set out to find the answer by changing the atmosphere around these communities and tracking how the trees responded over 11 years. The experiment, known as Aspen-FACE, was conducted in Rhinelander, Wisconsin, and exposed forest plots to elevated carbon dioxide (CO₂), elevated ozone (O₃), or both. According to the study by Alan F. Talhelm and colleagues, published in Global Change Biology, elevated CO₂ increased cumulative net primary productivity by 39% over the 11-year experiment. Elevated ozone had the opposite effect, reducing cumulative productivity by 10%. The study also found that elevated CO₂ increased total ecosystem carbon by 11%, while elevated ozone reduced it by 9%.Changing the forest airThe Aspen-FACE experiment began in 1998 and continued until 2009, giving researchers an unusually long opportunity to observe how forests respond to changing atmospheric conditions. Scientists used large circular plots to expose trees to controlled concentrations of CO₂ and ozone under open-air conditions. The forest communities included aspen, birch and maple, representing species found in northern temperate forests. Rather than examining plants in a laboratory or greenhouse, the experiment allowed the trees to grow outdoors while researchers altered the air surrounding them. This helped scientists study atmospheric effects under more realistic forest conditions.CO₂ boosted productivityThe strongest growth response came from elevated carbon dioxide. After 11 years, forests exposed to elevated CO₂ had 39% greater cumulative net primary productivity than forests under normal atmospheric conditions. Net primary productivity measures the amount of plant biomass produced by an ecosystem after accounting for the carbon plants use during respiration.The researchers found that elevated CO₂ also increased canopy nitrogen and nitrogen productivity. Trees accounted for approximately 95% of the cumulative productivity measured during the experiment. The increase extended to carbon storage. Total ecosystem carbon content was 11% higher under elevated CO₂. Tree carbon increased substantially, particularly in woody parts such as stems, branches and coarse roots. These findings showed that forests can maintain a significant productivity response to elevated CO₂ over a period much longer than a single growing season.Ozone worked differentlyGround-level ozone produced a contrasting result. Elevated ozone reduced cumulative net primary productivity by 10% over the 11-year period. The researchers linked this decline partly to reduced canopy nitrogen, which fell by 21% under elevated ozone. Ozone also reduced total ecosystem carbon by 9%. Unlike atmospheric CO₂, which plants use during photosynthesis, ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that can damage vegetation and interfere with plant growth.However, the ozone effect was not equally strong throughout the entire experiment. Researchers found that its negative effect on productivity became smaller as the forest developed, showing that trees and forest communities can respond differently as they mature.The combined effectThe interaction between the two gases was more complicated than simply adding their individual effects together. Although elevated CO₂ increased productivity by 39% and elevated ozone reduced it by 10%, the researchers found no statistically significant interaction between the treatments for cumulative net primary productivity. This means the study does not show that ozone directly cancelled a specific percentage of the CO₂-driven increase. Instead, the gases produced opposing effects, with CO₂ stimulating productivity and ozone placing pressure on forest growth. The combined treatment also produced an important result for carbon storage: ecosystem carbon under elevated CO₂ and ozone together was not significantly different from the ambient treatment.What it meansThe Wisconsin experiment offers a long-term look at how forests may respond to changing atmospheric conditions. Its findings show that rising CO₂ can stimulate forest productivity, but other atmospheric pollutants can work in the opposite direction. A later USDA Forest Service study used landscape modelling to examine how the Aspen-FACE findings could translate beyond the experimental plots. It found that CO₂ was the dominant driver of landscape response, while ozone had a significant negative effect on mean landscape biomass.The results underline why forests cannot be viewed simply as automatic carbon sinks. Their response depends on multiple environmental factors, including atmospheric composition, species, competition and forest development. After 11 years of changing the air around a Wisconsin forest, the scientists found a clear contrast: extra CO₂ encouraged productivity, while ozone limited growth and complicated the forest's carbon response.

articles.title: Aparece en el desierto de Nevada una Torre Eiffel de 50 metros partida por la mitad, obra de un artista francés: "Da miedo. Parece el fin del mundo"
articles.standfirst: La instalación, de grandes dimensiones de alto, pesa 30 toneladas
articles.summary: La instalación, de grandes dimensiones de alto, pesa 30 toneladas
articles.body: Una imagen difícil de creer está llamando la atención desde el desierto de Nevada: una enorme Torre Eiffel yace partida en dos sobre la arena de Black Rock City. No es el famoso monumento parisino, sino una gigantesca instalación artística creada especialmente para Burning Man 2026, el festival que cada año convierte durante unos días el desierto en una ciudad llena de obras imposibles. La escultura se llama Eiffela Broken Dream y es obra del artista francés Philippe Maindron. Se trata de una reproducción a escala 1:10 de la Torre Eiffel, construida en acero y formada por unas 5.000 piezas metálicas. La estructura tiene 15 metros de altura y 30 de longitud, y pesa alrededor de 30 toneladas. Maindron ha planteado la obra como una Torre Eiffel que parece haber caído después de un largo viaje y haberse partido al aterrizar en el desierto. Una de las partes permanece apoyada sobre sus cuatro patas, mientras la otra queda separada y apunta hacia el cielo. La instalación busca representar la caída de una civilización, pero también la posibilidad de empezar de nuevo. El proyecto fue seleccionado entre unas 500 propuestas para formar parte de la edición de este año de Burning Man. Además de contemplarla, los asistentes pueden interactuar con la instalación: un cable une las dos partes de la torre y está pensado para que un equilibrista pueda atravesarla. La elección del lugar tampoco es casual. Burning Man se celebra en el Black Rock Desert y reúne cada año a decenas de miles de personas alrededor de grandes instalaciones artísticas, música, performances y propuestas creadas por los propios participantes. La edición de 2026 se desarrolla entre el 30 de agosto y el 7 de septiembre. La enorme Torre Eiffel comparte este año espacio con otras construcciones monumentales, entre ellas un barco hundido de grandes dimensiones y el Temple of the Moon. El resultado vuelve a demostrar por qué Burning Man se ha convertido en uno de los escenarios más sorprendentes para el arte contemporáneo.

images.caption: Burning Man en Nevada, Estados Unidos EFE

articles.title: The rocket problem India cannot launch away
articles.summary: Science News: India has never had more rockets to talk about. The PSLV remains the backbone of the country's launch programme, notwithstanding its recent failures. .
articles.body: India has never had more rockets to talk about. The PSLV remains the backbone of the country's launch programme, notwithstanding its recent failures. GSLV-Mk2, like the one that launched Friday, gave India the ability to put heavier satellites into geostationary transfer orbit. LVM-3 has expanded India’s reach further and will carry some of the country’s most demanding missions. SSLV is being positioned as a quicker route to orbit for smaller satellites. Beyond them lie upgrades, reusable launch technologies and the Next Generation Launch Vehicle, or NGLV, on which India is betting for the next phase of its space programme.The private sector has begun adding to that picture too. Skyroot Aerospace has now put Vikram-1 into orbit, becoming the first Indian private company to achieve an orbital launch. Agnikul is pursuing its own orbital vehicle and a different propulsion architecture. More companies are entering the wider launch ecosystem.On the surface, then, India does not appear to have a rocket problem. But the question facing the country is no longer whether it can build rockets. It clearly can. The question is whether it can build enough access to space for everything it now wants to do there.Those are not the same thing. A capable rocket programme can still fall short if it cannot launch often enough. New vehicles do not automatically solve a capacity problem if they carry different classes of payload. More rockets on the drawing board do not necessarily translate into more launches if production, launchpads and associated infrastructure do not expand with them. And a failure that temporarily affects one vehicle can become a larger problem when too much of the system depends on the same facilities, technologies or people.That is the distinction India needs to confront as its space ambitions grow. The country is no longer planning only occasional planetary missions and satellite launches. The manifest ahead includes Chandrayaan-4, human spaceflight, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, large Earth-observation and communication satellites, navigation systems and strategic spacecraft. These are not all missions that can be squeezed onto a small rocket when one becomes available. Many require medium- or heavy-lift capability, and some have to fly on Indian launch vehicles.The challenge, therefore, is not merely one of launch frequency. It is also one of mass. India has, over the past decade, averaged about five orbital launches a year. Even under optimistic assumptions about planned upgrades, production improvements and additional private launchers, the available analysis suggests the country could struggle to generate the cadence required by its declared programme through 2030.Commercial ambitions face the same constraint. The PSLV built India a reputation as a reliable and affordable launch provider, but commercial customers look at access too, not just heritage. In an increasingly competitive market, India needs enough launch opportunities, across enough payload classes, for customers to plan around its schedule rather than wait for a slot.Cadence and capability, therefore, are commercial questions too. Small launchers may open new opportunities, but they cannot by themselves sustain India’s larger launch ambitions or replace medium- and heavy-lift capacity. If India wants launch services to become a meaningful part of its space economy, it will need to launch frequently and competitively across classes, not treat commercial launches as occasional additions to its national programme.The issue becomes clearer when measured against payload mass: a growing number of India's planned missions require capabilities that small launch vehicles simply cannot replace. This is why Skyroot’s success, important as it is, needs to be viewed at the right scale.Vikram-1 will one day be able to carry roughly 300-350 kg to low-Earth orbit — it is yet to demonstrate that payload capacity. Once that capacity is achieved, it’ll broadly be in the same small-lift class as Isro’s SSLV (tech transfer deal with HAL has been finalised). It creates an additional Indian route to orbit, particularly for smaller payloads, and its successful first flight is an achievement that should not be diminished.But India’s launch requirement is increasingly heavier than that. A PSLV can carry several times Vikram-1’s payload, while LVM-3 operates in an altogether different class. Chandrayaan-4, large satellite systems, human spaceflight and the infrastructure required for a future space station cannot be made easier simply by adding more small rockets to the fleet.This is not an argument against private launch vehicles. It is an argument against expecting one category of vehicle to solve another category’s problem.In fact, the emergence of Skyroot and other companies makes this moment an opportunity as much as a warning. India could, for the first time, begin building a genuinely broader launch ecosystem, in which private companies add capacity rather than merely compete for the same small segment of the market or depend indefinitely on Isro's infrastructure.That will require more than access to technology and launch facilities. India needs additional launch infrastructure, independent of the facilities on which its existing programme depends. The planned small-launch complex at Kulasekarapattinam is important in that context, but it will not, by itself, resolve the medium- and heavy-lift challenge.Production capacity must rise with demand. Propulsion research has to extend beyond the traditional institutions. And private companies will need customers capable of sustaining them through the long period between proving that a rocket can fly and proving that it can become a repeatable business.The govt, in other words, cannot simply announce that the private sector has arrived and then retreat from the launch business. That brings us to the intervention this week by nine employee bodies representing Isro and Department of Space staff.Their representation, seeking written clarity on the future role of Isro in launch-vehicle design, realisation, integration, testing and launch, is not merely a labour question. It has raised a larger institutional issue that India should address with considerably more clarity than it has so far.What exactly is the launch architecture the country wants? There is nothing contradictory about a strong public space agency and an expanding private industry. Indeed, India will need both. But there is a difference between transferring technology, expanding industrial production and creating new private capability on the one hand, and progressively hollowing out the institution that developed and still sustains the country’s most complex launch capabilities on the other.The distinction matters especially now because no Indian private company is yet building a PSLV-class vehicle, let alone something comparable to LVM-3 or NGLV. If Isro is expected to move away from manufacturing and operations, the transition cannot be treated as a matter of ideology or aspiration. It needs a credible answer to a practical question: who will guarantee that India has the launch capacity it needs while the private sector develops the capability to add its own?That answer should not be “wait and see”. The recent problems with PSLV illustrate why. The failures are not, by themselves, evidence of a broken programme. Rocket failures happen, including in mature launch systems. The more revealing issue is the extent to which a disruption in one part of India’s launch architecture can affect the wider programme. A resilient spacefaring nation needs not only reliable rockets, but enough production capacity, launch infrastructure and alternatives to absorb setbacks without allowing its entire schedule to drift.That is where India's current crisis and opportunity meet. The country should not respond by protecting Isro from competition. Nor should it respond by assuming that private competition makes Isro less necessary. It needs to increase the total amount of launch capacity available to the country, while creating greater redundancy between vehicles and infrastructure.Isro should remain capable of developing and flying the launch vehicles on which India’s scientific, strategic and human spaceflight programmes depend. Industry should be enabled to manufacture more, develop independently and eventually compete where it is capable of doing so. Private launch companies should have incentives to build vehicles and infrastructure that add new capacity rather than simply occupy a corner of an existing public system.The direction of travel matters because the rest of the world is not standing still. The global launch business is moving towards higher cadence, larger constellations, greater reusability and lower costs. China and the US are expanding both state-backed and commercial capacity, albeit through very different systems. India does not have to reproduce either model. But it does need to recognise that occasional demonstrations of capability are no longer enough.Access to space is becoming an industrial capability in its own right. India has spent decades learning to build rockets and, in the process, built an enviable launch heritage. The task ahead is different. It is to turn that heritage into a system capable of carrying an expanding national programme while also creating room for a private industry that can stand on its own.That will require more than one successful startup launch, more than one new rocket and more than another policy announcement. It will require capacity.--PostscriptFor decades, India’s space programme has taught us to look at a rocket and ask a simple question: how much can it carry? Perhaps the Parallax India now needs in its space story is the more important question: how often India can rely on it to carry the country where it says it wants to go.

articles.title: MIT researchers drilled a 2-by-3-foot hole through 3.6 feet of Arctic sea ice and sent a robot below; the prototype transmitted data through the ice at 1.2 kilobytes per second
articles.summary: Science News: The Arctic sea is becoming noisier and harder to reach. Beneath its frozen surface, cracking ice, marine mammals and passing ships create a constantly.
articles.body: The Arctic sea is becoming noisier and harder to reach. Beneath its frozen surface, cracking ice, marine mammals and passing ships create a constantly changing underwater soundscape. For scientists trying to understand this remote environment, the challenge is not simply listening. It is finding ways to place sensors beneath the ice and retrieve their data without repeatedly sending people into dangerous conditions. According to a report published by MIT News, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, researchers from MIT Lincoln Laboratory are working on both problems. During the U.S. Navy's Operation Ice Camp 2026, the team tested a prototype communications system designed to send data through Arctic sea ice using magnetic fields. After drilling through 3.6 feet of ice, researchers lowered a remotely operated vehicle into the water and achieved through ice data transmission at approximately 1.2 kilobytes per second. The MIT team has been developing a network of relatively inexpensive sensors capable of monitoring the Arctic continuously. The effort began with experiments during Operation Ice Camp 2024, when researchers deployed commercial off-the-shelf sensors and detected sounds including marine-mammal vocalizations. In 2026, the team returned with a higher-fidelity geophone capable of detecting vibrations traveling through sea ice. Understanding these sounds could become increasingly important as Arctic ice continues to break up and retreat. Fracturing ice produces distinctive acoustic signatures, while increased access to previously difficult-to-navigate waters could bring more ships and other activity into the region. A better understanding of the Arctic's acoustic environment could therefore support scientific monitoring, infrastructure planning, environmental resilience and maritime awareness.A mission complicated by extreme weatherGetting technology onto the ice proved almost as challenging as developing it. The 2026 Operation Ice Camp deployment was battered by consecutive blizzards, whiteout conditions, temperatures around minus 25 degrees Fahrenheit and winds of 25 to 30 mph, with gusts reaching 40 mph. Flights into the temporary Arctic camp were delayed for a week. Once the researchers finally arrived, another five-day period passed without a single flight arriving or departing. The team managed to deploy only about a quarter of its planned sensor package before deteriorating weather forced them to return to camp. The experience highlighted a central problem with Arctic research: even the most carefully planned fieldwork can be dictated by weather.Sending data through the iceWhile the sensor deployment was limited, researchers were also testing a different technology that could eventually reduce the need for people to work directly on the ice. The team partnered with Norwegian defense technology company Havguard to test a modem that communicates through ice using magnetic fields rather than radio-frequency signals. Radio signals are rapidly weakened by seawater, making conventional wireless communication difficult underwater. At a lagoon near Utqiaġvik, Alaska, researchers drilled a 2-by-3-foot opening through 3.6 feet of sea ice. A remotely operated vehicle carrying the underwater portion of the modem was then lowered beneath the ice. The system used a magneto-inductive transmitter underwater and a receiver positioned above the ice. Researchers also equipped the robot with a Doppler velocity logger and four-beam sonar, allowing them to track its movement beneath the frozen surface. The prototype achieved a data-transfer rate of approximately 1.2 kilobytes per second.Toward remote Arctic sensor networksThe result is an early but promising demonstration. The researchers envision future versions of the system collecting information from underwater sensors and relaying it to the outside world through drones or satellites. That could enable sensor networks to operate for longer periods while reducing the number of people required to travel onto unstable sea ice. The team is also exploring air-droppable versions of its sensors and plans to continue refining the modem's packaging and integration with its broader sensor system ahead of Operation Ice Camp 2028.Building technology for an unforgiving environmentThe project also extends beyond engineering. During their time in Utqiaġvik, researchers participated in local community events and worked with middle-school students on Arctic research and basic sonar concepts. Their experience has reinforced a simple lesson: Arctic technology must work in conditions where humans cannot always safely operate. The long-term goal is therefore not simply to send a robot beneath the ice. It is to create systems that can deploy sensors, communicate with them and retrieve their data while keeping people off the ice as much as possible. In a region where weather can shut down an entire operation for days, that capability could prove as valuable as the sensors themselves.Images Courtesy: MIT News

articles.title: A five-year Illinois project will restore 421 acres of wetlands, prairie and woodland while helping hold stormwater, part of an $11 million effort along 67 miles of river
articles.summary: Science News: What if a landscape could act like a giant sponge, soaking up stormwater, filtering pollution and creating space for wildlife all at once? Sounds impo.
articles.body: What if a landscape could act like a giant sponge, soaking up stormwater, filtering pollution and creating space for wildlife all at once? Sounds impossible? Well, that is the goal behind a major five-year restoration project planned at Raven Glen Forest Preserve in Antioch, Illinois. According to a report by Lake County Forest Preserve, the project will restore 421 acres of wetlands, prairies and woodlands, while reshaping the landscape to better manage stormwater and improve the health of the surrounding watershed. It has been reported tat the work is expected to begin this fall or winter and will focus on land east of Savage Road and west of Route 45. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ Chicago District is leading the project in partnership with the Lake County Forest Preserves. For the uninitiated, the Raven Glen work is part of a much larger federal initiative focused on restoring ecosystems and reducing flooding risks along 67 miles of the Des Plaines River in Lake and Cook counties. The broader watershed effort is backed by $11 million secured by U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin. At Raven Glen, crews will concentrate on Hastings Creek and wetlands at the southern end of the preserve.Turning farmland back into wetlandsAccording to the report, the area has a long agricultural history. It operated as a dairy farm until the late 1990s, with its farmstead regarded as state-of-the-art during the 1950s and 1960s. But farming had altered the natural flow of water. Underground drainage tiles were installed to move water away from fields, while Hastings Creek was modified to support agricultural operations. The restoration will reverse many of those changes. Crews will disable the drainage tiles, reshape sections of the land and reconnect Hastings Creek with its floodplain. They will also restore the creek's natural curves and introduce shallow, rocky sections known as riffles.A natural defense against floodingThe restored wetlands and floodplain will be able to hold stormwater for longer periods and release it more gradually. That could reduce pressure on downstream areas while improving water quality throughout the Upper Des Plaines River Watershed. The project will also remove invasive vegetation and introduce native seeds and seedlings. The work is designed to rebuild a variety of habitats, including marshes, meadows, prairies and woodlands.Expanding a protected wildlife landscapeRaven Glen covers 604 acres and is known for its rolling terrain, wetlands and oak-hickory groves. Its connection to the 501-acre Ethel's Woods Forest Preserve through a pedestrian tunnel beneath Route 45 creates an expansive stretch of protected habitat. The restoration could strengthen that connected landscape, providing better conditions for wildlife while improving its ability to absorb and manage water.Trails to remain openDespite the scale of the work, visitors will still be able to access Raven Glen during construction. The preserve and its trails are expected to remain open, although brief temporary closures may be necessary for visitor safety. By restoring the land's natural ability to store water, filter runoff and support native ecosystems, the project aims to make Raven Glen more resilient for both people and wildlife, turning a landscape once engineered for farming back toward the natural systems that shaped it.
